question: Which statement about heapsort is true?
options: It is stable and runs in O(n) time
Its worst case is O(n^2) like quicksort
It runs in O(n log n) worst case and is in-place but not stable
It requires O(n) auxiliary space
explanation: Heapsort sorts within the array with guaranteed O(n log n) time, but swaps can reorder equal keys.

question: Why does the greedy value-to-weight strategy fail for 0/1 knapsack even though it works for fractional knapsack?
options: 0/1 knapsack has negative weights
Fractional knapsack is NP-hard
Greedy cannot sort items by ratio
Items cannot be split, so taking the best-ratio item may waste capacity a better combination would use
explanation: Without fractions, leftover capacity can make a locally best choice globally suboptimal.

question: Compared with a red-black tree, what is characteristic of an AVL tree?
options: It allows duplicate keys while red-black trees do not
It is less balanced but never needs rotations
It is more strictly balanced, giving faster lookups but possibly more rotations on updates
It guarantees O(1) insertion
explanation: AVL height stays near 1.44 log n versus about 2 log n for red-black trees, at the cost of more rebalancing.

options: O(n * n!)
O(n!) / n

question: Why is the O(n * W) 0/1 knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial?
options: Its runtime is polynomial in the value W but exponential in the number of bits needed to encode W
It uses polynomial space but exponential time
It is polynomial only when n is less than W
It runs in polynomial time only on average
explanation: Input size counts the bits of W, so doubling the bit length can square W's magnitude.

question: In an efficient N-Queens backtracking solution, how are conflicts usually checked in O(1) per placement?
options: By rescanning the entire board after each placement
By sorting the queens by row after each step
By tracking occupied columns and both diagonal directions in sets or boolean arrays
By precomputing all N! permutations first
explanation: Columns, row - col, and row + col identify attacking lines, so a lookup tells whether a square is safe.

question: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
options: It uses less memory per node
Removing a node given a direct reference is O(1) because its predecessor is known
